MS-1.t: Trace the fate of somites from paraxial mesoderm into sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle), and dermatome (dermis), and relate epaxial muscles to dorsal rami and hypaxial muscles to ventral rami.
Explain resegmentation, in which each vertebral body forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next, and identify the notochord remnant as the nucleus pulposus.

Relate limb patterning signals to limb defects: FGF from the apical ectodermal ridge (proximal to distal outgrowth), sonic hedgehog from the zone of polarizing activity (anterior to posterior patterning; ectopic expression causes polydactyly), HOX genes (segment identity), and thalidomide (phocomelia).
MS-1.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Congenital disorders: disorders of limb development (HOX gene mutation, phocomelia)

MS-1.t: Explain why the upper limb rotates laterally and the lower limb rotates medially during development, and use this to predict the position of flexor and extensor compartments and the spiral dermatome pattern of the leg.

Compare intramembranous ossification (flat bones of the skull vault, most of the clavicle) with endochondral ossification (hyaline cartilage model, primary center in the diaphysis, secondary centers in the epiphyses), and describe how joints form from interzone mesenchyme by cavitation.

Match pharyngeal arch muscles to their nerves: first arch (muscles of mastication, CN V3), second arch (muscles of facial expression, CN VII), third arch (stylopharyngeus, CN IX), fourth and sixth arches (pharynx and larynx, CN X).

MS-2.t: Identify the A band, I band, H zone, M line, and Z line of the sarcomere, and predict which bands shorten during contraction (I band and H zone) and which stays constant (A band).

Distinguish skeletal muscle (multinucleate, peripheral nuclei, triads), cardiac muscle (branched, central nuclei, intercalated discs with gap junctions and desmosomes, dyads), and smooth muscle (fusiform, central nucleus, dense bodies, no striations) on histology.

Describe compact bone (osteons with central Haversian canals, Volkmann canals, concentric lamellae, osteocytes in lacunae linked by canaliculi) and spongy bone (trabeculae surrounding marrow), and distinguish woven from lamellar bone.

Compare osteoblasts (mesenchymal origin, secrete type I collagen osteoid and alkaline phosphatase), osteocytes (mechanosensing, FGF23 secretion), and osteoclasts (monocyte and macrophage lineage, multinucleated, ruffled border, acid and cathepsin K in Howship lacunae).

Describe the epiphyseal growth plate zones (reserve, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, ossification) and predict how defects in chondrocyte proliferation (achondroplasia) or mineralization (rickets) alter the plate.

Distinguish fibrous joints (sutures, syndesmoses, gomphoses), cartilaginous joints (hyaline synchondroses, fibrocartilage symphyses such as the pubic symphysis and intervertebral disc), and synovial joints (avascular articular hyaline cartilage, synoviocytes producing hyaluronan and lubricin).

MS-3.t: Identify regional vertebral features: cervical transverse foramina and bifid spines, the atlas (no body) and axis (dens), thoracic costal facets, and large lumbar bodies, and explain how each relates to regional function.

Distinguish the normal cervical and lumbar lordosis and thoracic kyphosis from scoliosis (lateral curvature with vertebral rotation) and excessive kyphosis, and predict how severe thoracic scoliosis restricts lung expansion.
MS-3.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: kyphoscoliosis, scoliosis

MS-3.t: Locate the major skull foramina and their contents (superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, internal acoustic meatus, jugular foramen, foramen magnum), and explain why a pterion fracture can tear the middle meningeal artery.

Describe the clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, and carpal bones, and predict the nerve at risk with fractures of the humeral surgical neck (axillary), radial groove (radial), and medial epicondyle (ulnar).

Describe the hip bone (ilium, ischium, pubis fused at the acetabulum), femur, tibia, fibula, and foot arches, relate a collapsed medial longitudinal arch to flat foot (pes planus), and predict common fibular nerve injury with a fibular neck fracture.
MS-3.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Congenital disorders: foot deformities (flat foot)

MS-4.t: Classify joints by function (synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, diarthrosis) and synovial joints by type (hinge, pivot, ball and socket, saddle, condyloid, plane), giving an example of each such as the atlantoaxial pivot and first carpometacarpal saddle.

Apply Hilton law (nerves to muscles acting on a joint also supply the joint) to explain articular proprioception and nociception, and why hip disease can present as knee pain through the obturator and femoral nerves.
Explain why the glenohumeral joint depends on the rotator cuff for stability, and predict axillary nerve injury and loss of deltoid abduction after anterior shoulder dislocation.

Relate knee ligaments and menisci to clinical tests: anterior drawer and Lachman (ACL), posterior drawer (PCL), valgus stress (MCL), varus stress (LCL), and explain why the medial meniscus, attached to the MCL, is injured more often.

Describe the temporomandibular joint (synovial joint with an articular disc, hinge and gliding movement, innervated by auriculotemporal and masseteric branches of CN V3) and relate disc displacement to clicking and jaw pain.
MS-4.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Inflammatory disorders: temporomandibular joint disorders

MS-5.t: Describe the rotator cuff muscles: supraspinatus (initial abduction, suprascapular nerve), infraspinatus (lateral rotation, suprascapular nerve), teres minor (lateral rotation, axillary nerve), subscapularis (medial rotation, subscapular nerves), and identify supraspinatus as most often injured.
MS-5.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: rotator cuff syndrome

MS-5.t: Predict upper limb deficits from nerve injury: musculocutaneous (weak elbow flexion), radial (wrist drop), median (loss of thenar opposition, ape hand), ulnar (claw hand, weak finger abduction), and long thoracic (winged scapula from serratus anterior paralysis).

Predict lower limb deficits from nerve injury: femoral (weak knee extension), obturator (weak adduction), superior gluteal (Trendelenburg sign with pelvic drop on the opposite side), common fibular (foot drop, weak eversion), and tibial (weak plantarflexion and inversion).

Describe the action and innervation of head and neck muscles: muscles of mastication (CN V3), muscles of facial expression (CN VII), tongue muscles (CN XII, except palatoglossus by CN X), and sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (CN XI).

Describe trunk muscles: erector spinae (extension, dorsal rami), diaphragm (inspiration, phrenic nerve C3 to C5), anterior abdominal wall layers (thoracoabdominal and subcostal nerves), and levator ani (pelvic floor support).

MS-6.t: Trace musculoskeletal connective tissue origins: limb bones, cartilage, and tendons from lateral plate (somatic) mesoderm, axial skeleton from sclerotome, and craniofacial bone and cartilage largely from neural crest mesenchyme.

Match collagen types to tissues: type I (bone, tendon, ligament, fibrocartilage), type II (hyaline cartilage, nucleus pulposus), type III (reticular fibers, vessels, granulation tissue), and type IV (basement membrane).

Sequence collagen synthesis (Gly-X-Y chains, proline and lysine hydroxylation requiring vitamin C, triple helix formation, propeptide cleavage, lysyl oxidase cross-linking requiring copper) and predict the defect at each step in scurvy, osteogenesis imperfecta, and Menkes disease.
Explain how articular cartilage resists compression (aggrecan with chondroitin and keratan sulfate on hyaluronan binding water) and why avascular cartilage and poorly vascular tendons heal slowly.
Describe elastic fibers (elastin cores on fibrillin-1 microfibrils) in elastic ligaments such as the ligamentum flavum, and explain how fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-beta.

MS-7.t: Trace skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling from T-tubule depolarization through the dihydropyridine receptor and its mechanical link to ryanodine receptor 1, calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, calcium binding to troponin C, and calcium reuptake by SERCA.
Sequence the cross-bridge cycle (ATP binding releases myosin from actin, hydrolysis cocks the head, phosphate release drives the power stroke) and explain rigor mortis as the loss of ATP.
Explain how skeletal muscle force is graded by motor unit recruitment (size principle) and summation to tetanus, and interpret length-tension and force-velocity relationships.

Explain calcium-induced calcium release through L-type channels and ryanodine receptor 2 in cardiac muscle, why its long refractory period prevents tetany, and how sympathetic stimulation increases contractility via phospholamban phosphorylation.

Explain smooth muscle contraction through calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase, relaxation by myosin light chain phosphatase, the latch state, and nitric oxide induced relaxation through cGMP.

Compare type I fibers (slow, oxidative, red, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, fatigue resistant) with type II fibers (fast, glycolytic, fatigable), and predict adaptations to endurance training (greater oxidative capacity) and resistance training (type II fiber hypertrophy).

MS-8.t: Trace vitamin D activation from 7-dehydrocholesterol in UVB-exposed skin through hepatic 25-hydroxylation and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation, and explain why serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D reflects vitamin D status.
MS-8.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin deficiencies: vitamin D

MS-8.t: Explain how PTH (bone resorption via osteoblast RANKL, distal tubule calcium reabsorption, phosphaturia, 1-alpha-hydroxylase activation), calcitriol, calcitonin, and osteocyte FGF23 regulate serum calcium and phosphate, and how osteoprotegerin limits osteoclast activation.

Compare muscle fuel use across exercise duration (phosphocreatine via creatine kinase, anaerobic glycolysis to lactate, oxidative metabolism of glucose and fatty acids) and explain the Cori cycle and creatinine as a marker of muscle mass.

Explain McArdle disease (autosomal recessive muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency) and predict exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria, failure of blood lactate to rise with exercise, and the second wind phenomenon.

Relate carnitine shuttle defects such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency to muscle weakness and exertional rhabdomyolysis during prolonged exercise or fasting, when muscle depends on fatty acid oxidation.

Explain mineral and cofactor roles in bone and muscle: magnesium for PTH secretion, copper for lysyl oxidase cross-linking, vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation of osteocalcin, and calcium hydroxyapatite as the bone mineral.

MS-9.t: Relate transcription factors to skeletal development: RUNX2 for osteoblast differentiation (haploinsufficiency causes cleidocranial dysplasia with absent clavicles and delayed suture closure), SOX9 for chondrocyte differentiation, and HOX genes for segment identity.
Explain how FGFR3 gain-of-function mutations inhibit chondrocyte proliferation in achondroplasia, and why most cases are new autosomal dominant mutations associated with advanced paternal age.

Explain the dominant-negative effect of glycine substitutions in COL1A1 or COL1A2 in severe osteogenesis imperfecta, compared with null alleles that halve normal collagen output and cause the milder type I form.

Apply the reading frame rule to dystrophin: frameshift deletions abolish dystrophin (Duchenne), while in-frame deletions produce a truncated, partly functional protein (Becker), and explain why the very large DMD gene has a high new mutation rate.
MS-9.usmle: Nervous System: Neuromuscular disorders: muscular dystrophy

MS-9.t: Explain myotonic dystrophy type 1 as an autosomal dominant CTG repeat expansion in DMPK showing anticipation, and predict myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy, and cardiac conduction defects.
Explain maternal inheritance and heteroplasmy in mitochondrial myopathies, and identify ragged red fibers on Gomori trichrome stain in disorders such as MERRF and MELAS.

Relate cell cycle and oncogene defects to bone and soft tissue sarcomas: RB1 loss (osteosarcoma after hereditary retinoblastoma), TP53 loss in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion transcription factor from t(11;22) in Ewing sarcoma.

MS-10.t: Trace neuromuscular transmission (calcium entry, SNARE-mediated acetylcholine release, nicotinic receptor end plate potential, acetylcholinesterase) and localize the defect in myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, and botulism.

Distinguish myasthenia gravis (anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, weakness that worsens with use, ptosis and diplopia) from Lambert-Eaton syndrome (anti-presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, strength improving with repeated effort, small cell lung cancer).
MS-10.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: myasthenia gravis

MS-10.t: Compare muscle spindles (Ia afferents, stretch reflex, gamma motor neuron tuning) with Golgi tendon organs (Ib afferents, tension sensing), and match reflexes to roots: biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1.

Distinguish neurogenic weakness (fasciculations, grouped atrophy, fiber type grouping, as in spinal muscular atrophy from SMN1 deletion) from myopathic weakness (proximal weakness, elevated CK), and identify type II fiber atrophy from disuse or corticosteroids.
MS-10.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: muscles, ligaments, fascia: muscle wasting and diffuse atrophy

MS-10.t: Explain why hypocalcemia increases nerve and muscle excitability (lower sodium channel threshold), producing tetany with Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and why hypokalemia and hyperkalemia both cause muscle weakness.

MS-11.t: Explain rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis: HLA-DR4 associated autoimmunity to citrullinated peptides, CD4 T cell and cytokine (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) driven synovitis, and pannus with RANKL-driven osteoclasts eroding cartilage and bone.

Distinguish rheumatoid arthritis (symmetric MCP and PIP synovitis sparing the DIP, morning stiffness over 1 hour, ulnar deviation, swan neck deformity, nodules, anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor) from osteoarthritis, and identify Felty syndrome (RA, splenomegaly, neutropenia).
MS-11.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Immunologic disorders: rheumatoid arthritis, Felty syndrome

MS-11.t: Match autoantibodies to rheumatic diseases: anti-CCP (rheumatoid arthritis), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (SLE), anti-Scl-70 (diffuse systemic sclerosis), anticentromere (limited systemic sclerosis), anti-U1 RNP (mixed connective tissue disease), anti-Jo-1 (myositis), anti-SSA and anti-SSB (Sjogren syndrome).

Describe musculoskeletal features of SLE (nonerosive arthritis), systemic sclerosis (sclerodactyly, calcinosis, flexion contractures, Raynaud phenomenon), and mixed connective tissue disease (overlapping SLE, scleroderma, and myositis features with anti-U1 RNP).

Classify hypersensitivity in musculoskeletal disease: type II in rheumatic fever polyarthritis (molecular mimicry) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies against small cell lung cancer cross-reacting with presynaptic calcium channels), type III in SLE arthritis, and type IV in polymyositis.

Explain innate immune activation in joints: urate crystals activating the NLRP3 inflammasome to release IL-1 beta in gout, and neutrophil proteases destroying articular cartilage within days in septic arthritis.

Describe postinfectious and postvaccine arthritis: HLA-B27 associated reactive arthritis after enteric or chlamydial infection, symmetric small joint arthritis after parvovirus B19 or rubella infection, and transient arthralgia in adult women after rubella vaccination.

MS-12.t: Describe Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase and coagulase positive) and explain how protein A, collagen and fibronectin adhesins, and biofilm on hardware make it the most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.
MS-12.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Infectious disorders: osteomyelitis, septic arthritis

MS-12.t: Describe Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococci; pili with antigenic variation, IgA protease) and the disseminated gonococcal infection pattern of tenosynovitis, pustular dermatitis, and migratory polyarthralgia or purulent monoarthritis in sexually active young adults.

Match osteomyelitis organisms to settings: Salmonella (sickle cell disease), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (injection drug use, puncture through a shoe sole), Pasteurella multocida (cat and dog bites), Staphylococcus epidermidis (prosthetic material), and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (vertebrae).

Describe Clostridium perfringens (gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming rod) and explain how alpha toxin (phospholipase C, lecithinase) destroys cell membranes, producing myonecrosis, gas, and hemolysis in contaminated deep wounds.

Describe Streptococcus pyogenes (beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains) and explain how M protein resists phagocytosis while hyaluronidase, streptokinase, and superantigen pyrogenic exotoxins promote spread along fascia and toxic shock.

Describe Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete) and its transmission cycle, in which Ixodes larvae acquire it from white-footed mice and nymphs transmit it after about 36 hours or more of attachment, and the late Lyme arthritis of large joints, especially the knee.
MS-12.usmle: Multisystem: Infectious disorders: bacterial: Lyme disease

MS-12.t: Explain how Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads hematogenously to vertebral bodies (Pott disease), forming caseating granulomas that collapse adjacent vertebrae and disc space, producing gibbus deformity and psoas abscess.

MS-13-A.t: Explain how vitamin D deficiency or phosphate loss causes defective mineralization of osteoid, producing rickets before growth plate closure and osteomalacia after it.
MS-13-A.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin deficiencies: vitamin D (rickets)

MS-13-A.t: Identify risk factors for vitamin D deficiency: limited sun exposure, darker skin, unsupplemented exclusive breastfeeding, fat malabsorption, liver or kidney disease, and anticonvulsant use.
MS-13-A.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin deficiencies: vitamin D (rickets)

MS-13-A.t: Describe osteomalacia findings: diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, Looser zones (pseudofractures), and labs showing low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
MS-13-A.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: osteomalacia

MS-13-A.t: Describe rickets findings: rachitic rosary, craniotabes, frontal bossing, bowed legs (genu varum), widened and cupped metaphyses on radiograph, and distinguish X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets caused by FGF23 excess.
MS-13-A.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin deficiencies: vitamin D (rickets)

MS-13-A.t: Explain how vitamin C deficiency impairs prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation, producing unstable collagen triple helices, fragile vessels, and poor wound healing.
MS-13-A.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin deficiencies: vitamin C (scurvy)

MS-13-A.t: Describe scurvy findings and risks: perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, poor wound healing, hemarthrosis, and painful subperiosteal hemorrhage in children, in people with diets lacking fruit and vegetables or with alcohol use disorder.
MS-13-A.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin deficiencies: vitamin C (scurvy)

MS-13-B.t: Explain ankylosing spondylitis as an HLA-B27 associated seronegative spondyloarthropathy with enthesitis and sacroiliitis, and predict inflammatory back pain in young men that improves with exercise, reduced chest expansion, and bamboo spine from syndesmophytes.
Identify extra-articular complications of ankylosing spondylitis: anterior uveitis, aortitis with aortic regurgitation, restrictive lung disease, and vertebral fractures in a fused spine.

Describe bursitis by site and cause, including prepatellar bursitis from kneeling, olecranon bursitis, subacromial and trochanteric bursitis from overuse, and septic bursitis from Staphylococcus aureus.

Explain fibromyalgia as a disorder of central pain sensitization, and identify widespread pain for at least 3 months with fatigue and unrefreshing sleep, most often in women, with normal inflammatory markers and CK.
MS-13-B.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Inflammatory disorders: fibrositis, myofascial pain syndrome

MS-13-B.t: Explain hyperuricemia in gout from urate underexcretion (most cases, thiazides, kidney disease) or overproduction (Lesch-Nyhan HGPRT deficiency, tumor lysis, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency), with xanthine oxidase converting hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid.
MS-13-B.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: joints: gout

MS-13-B.t: Identify gout findings: acute monoarthritis of the first MTP joint (podagra) triggered by alcohol or purine-rich meals, needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals, tophi, punched-out erosions, and uric acid kidney stones.
MS-13-B.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: joints: gout

MS-13-B.t: Distinguish dermatomyositis (complement-mediated capillary injury, perifascicular atrophy, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, association with internal cancer) from polymyositis (endomysial CD8 T cells), both with proximal weakness, high CK, and possible anti-Jo-1 interstitial lung disease.

Interpret muscle biopsy and laboratory findings to separate inflammatory myositis (high CK, inflammatory infiltrates, myofiber necrosis) from polymyalgia rheumatica (normal CK and strength) and steroid myopathy.

Describe polymyalgia rheumatica in adults over 50: pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles, elevated ESR, normal CK, and its association with giant cell (temporal) arteritis and risk of vision loss.
MS-13-B.usmle: Multisystem: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: polymyalgia rheumatica

MS-13-B.t: Explain reactive arthritis as an HLA-B27 associated sterile arthritis following Chlamydia trachomatis or enteric infection (Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter), presenting with arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, plus enthesitis and keratoderma blennorrhagicum.
MS-13-B.usmle: Multisystem: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: reactive arthritis

MS-13-B.t: Explain tendinopathy as overuse-induced collagen disorganization with limited inflammation (tendinosis), and identify lateral epicondylitis (extensor carpi radialis brevis origin), medial epicondylitis, and supraspinatus impingement with a painful arc.

Describe de Quervain tenosynovitis (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, positive Finkelstein test), plantar fasciitis, and Achilles tendinopathy with rupture risk increased by fluoroquinolones.
Distinguish psoriatic arthritis (DIP involvement, dactylitis, nail pitting, pencil-in-cup deformity, axial disease linked to HLA-B27) from rheumatoid arthritis.

Describe juvenile idiopathic arthritis (arthritis before age 16 lasting at least 6 weeks), including the oligoarticular ANA-positive form with silent anterior uveitis and the systemic form with daily spiking fever and salmon-colored rash.
MS-13-B.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Immunologic disorders: juvenile idiopathic arthritis

MS-13-B.t: Distinguish pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition, rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals, chondrocalcinosis, knee and wrist, linked to hyperparathyroidism and hemochromatosis) from gout.
MS-13-B.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: joints: pseudogout

MS-13-B.t: Describe adhesive capsulitis (capsular inflammation and fibrosis with loss of both active and passive shoulder motion, associated with diabetes) and ganglion cysts (myxoid degeneration near a joint capsule or tendon sheath, often the dorsal wrist, lacking a true lining).
MS-13-B.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Inflammatory disorders: adhesive capsulitis, ganglion cyst

MS-13-C.t: Explain osteopetrosis as failure of osteoclast bone resorption (for example carbonic anhydrase II deficiency with renal tubular acidosis, or CLCN7 mutations), producing dense but brittle bone.

Predict osteopetrosis complications: fractures, pancytopenia from marrow obliteration with extramedullary hematopoiesis and hepatosplenomegaly, and cranial nerve palsies (vision and hearing loss) from narrowed foramina, more severe in the infantile autosomal recessive form.

Interpret serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH to distinguish osteoporosis (all normal), osteomalacia, Paget disease (isolated high alkaline phosphatase), primary hyperparathyroidism, and renal osteodystrophy.
MS-13-C.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage

MS-13-C.t: Explain renal osteodystrophy: phosphate retention and low calcitriol in chronic kidney disease cause secondary hyperparathyroidism, with osteitis fibrosa cystica (subperiosteal resorption, brown tumors) and defective mineralization.
MS-13-C.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: osteodystrophy

MS-13-D.t: Explain Marfan syndrome as an autosomal dominant FBN1 (fibrillin-1) defect with excess TGF-beta signaling, and identify tall stature, arachnodactyly, arm span exceeding height, pectus deformity, joint hypermobility, and upward lens dislocation.
MS-13-D.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic disorders: structural protein disorders: Marfan syndrome

MS-13-D.t: Predict Marfan cardiovascular complications (aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, mitral valve prolapse) and distinguish Marfan from homocystinuria (downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, thrombosis).
MS-13-D.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic disorders: structural protein disorders: Marfan syndrome

MS-13-D.t: Describe Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked, absent dystrophin): onset before age 5, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy from fibrofatty replacement, markedly elevated CK, dilated cardiomyopathy, and respiratory failure.
MS-13-D.usmle: Nervous System: Neuromuscular disorders: muscular dystrophy

MS-13-D.t: Compare Becker muscular dystrophy (later onset, milder course, truncated dystrophin) with Duchenne, and use dystrophin immunostaining and genetic testing to separate them.
MS-13-D.usmle: Nervous System: Neuromuscular disorders: muscular dystrophy

MS-13-D.t: Explain osteogenesis imperfecta as defective type I collagen (COL1A1 or COL1A2), and identify multiple fractures with minimal trauma, blue sclerae, conductive hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and joint laxity.
Distinguish osteogenesis imperfecta from nonaccidental trauma in a child with multiple fractures using sclerae, dentition, family history, and fracture pattern.

Describe Ehlers-Danlos syndrome as a group of collagen disorders (classic type V collagen, vascular type III collagen) with skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and dislocation, easy bruising, and arterial or bowel rupture in the vascular type.
MS-13-D.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic disorders: structural protein disorders: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

MS-13-D.t: Identify achondroplasia findings: rhizomelic limb shortening with a normal-length trunk, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, and normal intelligence.

MS-13-E.t: Explain osteoarthritis pathogenesis (chondrocyte injury, proteoglycan loss, cartilage fibrillation, eburnation, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, osteophytes) and risk factors (age, obesity, prior joint injury, mechanical load).
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: joints: osteoarthritis

MS-13-E.t: Identify osteoarthritis findings: pain worse with use, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodes, asymmetric weight-bearing joint involvement, and radiographic joint space narrowing with osteophytes.
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: joints: osteoarthritis

MS-13-E.t: Explain osteoporosis as reduced bone mass with normal mineralization, driven by low peak bone mass, estrogen loss increasing RANKL-mediated resorption, aging, and secondary causes (glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism, immobilization, alcohol, smoking).
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: osteoporosis

MS-13-E.t: Interpret osteoporosis findings: vertebral compression, hip, and distal radius fractures, height loss and kyphosis, normal serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase, and DEXA T-scores of minus 2.5 or lower (osteopenia between minus 1 and minus 2.5).
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: osteoporosis, osteopenia

MS-13-E.t: Explain Paget disease of bone as osteoclast overactivity followed by disorganized osteoblastic repair (lytic, mixed, and sclerotic phases) producing thick but weak mosaic lamellar bone, with isolated elevation of alkaline phosphatase.
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: osteitis deformans (Paget disease of bone)

MS-13-E.t: Predict Paget disease complications in older adults: bone pain, enlarging skull, hearing loss, fractures, high-output heart failure from arteriovenous shunting, and osteosarcoma.
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: osteitis deformans (Paget disease of bone)

MS-13-E.t: Explain avascular necrosis as bone infarction from interrupted blood supply, and identify causes (glucocorticoids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, SLE, decompression sickness, femoral neck and scaphoid fractures) and the femoral head as the most common site.
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: osteonecrosis (avascular), bone infarct

MS-13-E.t: Distinguish pediatric hip disorders: developmental dysplasia of the hip (newborn, Ortolani and Barlow tests), Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (idiopathic femoral head osteonecrosis in young children), and slipped capital femoral epiphysis (obese adolescent, epiphysis slips off the femoral neck).
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease

MS-13-E.t: Relate disc degeneration to posterolateral nucleus pulposus herniation compressing the lower root (L4 to L5 herniation affects L5), and distinguish spondylosis (degenerative change) from spondylolisthesis (forward vertebral slip).
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: disc degeneration, herniated disc

MS-13-E.t: Distinguish adolescent knee disorders: Osgood-Schlatter disease (traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle), chondromalacia patellae (softened patellar cartilage with anterior knee pain), and osteochondritis dissecans (separation of a subchondral bone and cartilage fragment).
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: bone, tendon, cartilage: Osgood-Schlatter disease

MS-13-E.t: Describe Dupuytren contracture as myofibroblast proliferation in the palmar fascia causing flexion contracture of the ring and little fingers.
MS-13-E.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: muscles, ligaments, fascia: Dupuytren contracture

MS-13-F.t: Describe chondrosarcoma as a malignant cartilage-forming tumor of older adults in the pelvis, proximal femur, and shoulder girdle, which can arise from enchondroma or osteochondroma and often carries IDH1 or IDH2 mutations.

Describe Ewing sarcoma in children and adolescents: diaphyseal or pelvic tumor of small round blue cells, CD99 positive, EWSR1-FLI1 from t(11;22), onion-skin periosteal reaction, and fever that can mimic osteomyelitis.

Describe osteoid osteoma (under 2 cm cortical nidus with a sclerotic rim in young males, night pain relieved by NSAIDs because the nidus produces prostaglandin E2) and distinguish osteoblastoma (larger, vertebral).

Describe osteosarcoma as the most common primary malignant bone tumor apart from myeloma: malignant osteoid, metaphysis around the knee, peaks in adolescents and in older adults with Paget disease or prior radiation.
Interpret osteosarcoma imaging (Codman triangle, sunburst pattern), relate risk to RB1 and TP53 loss, and predict hematogenous metastasis to lung.

Describe rhabdomyosarcoma as the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood, arising in the head and neck or genitourinary tract (sarcoma botryoides), with desmin and myogenin positive rhabdomyoblasts and PAX3 or PAX7 to FOXO1 fusions in the alveolar type.

Distinguish benign cartilage tumors: osteochondroma (EXT1 or EXT2, metaphyseal bony stalk with a cartilage cap) and enchondroma (intramedullary hyaline cartilage in hand bones, multiple in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome), with risk of chondrosarcoma.

Describe giant cell tumor of bone (epiphyseal soap-bubble lesion in young adults, RANKL-expressing stromal cells with osteoclast-like giant cells) and tenosynovial giant cell tumor (synovial or tendon sheath tumor overexpressing CSF1).
MS-13-F.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Neoplasms: tenosynovial giant cell tumor

MS-13-F.t: Explain why metastases are the most common malignant bone tumors, distinguish osteoblastic (prostate), osteolytic (kidney, thyroid, lung), and mixed (breast) lesions, and predict pathologic fracture and hypercalcemia as complications.

Compare soft tissue sarcomas by lineage marker, rhabdomyosarcoma (desmin, myogenin) and leiomyosarcoma (smooth muscle actin, desmin; uterus and retroperitoneum in adults), and explain their hematogenous spread to lung.
Describe hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (digital clubbing, periosteal new bone formation, and arthritis) as a paraneoplastic syndrome of lung cancer.
MS-13-F.usmle: Multisystem: Paraneoplastic syndromes: musculoskeletal: pulmonary osteoarthropathy

MS-13-G.t: Explain septic arthritis pathogenesis (hematogenous seeding or direct inoculation, mostly Staphylococcus aureus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active adults) and risk factors (rheumatoid arthritis, prosthetic joints, injection drug use, diabetes).

Interpret synovial fluid analysis: noninflammatory (under 2,000 WBC/mm3), inflammatory, and septic (usually over 50,000 WBC/mm3 with neutrophils, positive Gram stain or culture), plus crystal identification, to evaluate an acute hot swollen joint.
MS-13-G.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: joints: joint effusion

MS-13-G.t: Explain necrotizing fasciitis as rapidly spreading infection along fascial planes, type I polymicrobial (diabetes, perineal Fournier gangrene) or type II Streptococcus pyogenes, with pain out of proportion to exam, crepitus, bullae, and systemic toxicity.

Explain why hematogenous osteomyelitis in children localizes to the metaphysis of long bones, and contrast contiguous spread from diabetic foot ulcers and vertebral osteomyelitis with discitis in adults.

Identify osteomyelitis findings and complications: sequestrum, involucrum, Brodie abscess, elevated ESR and CRP, MRI as the most sensitive imaging, chronic draining sinus, and squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic sinus tract.

Distinguish dry gangrene (coagulative necrosis after arterial occlusion, sharply demarcated) from wet gangrene (superimposed bacterial infection with liquefactive necrosis), and explain the higher risk in diabetes and peripheral artery disease.
MS-13-G.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Infectious disorders: gangrene, dry and wet

MS-13-G.t: Describe gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) after deep contaminated wounds: rapid spread, severe pain, crepitus from gas, bronze skin, hemolysis, and shock from Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin.

Describe infective myositis: pyomyositis (Staphylococcus aureus abscess in large muscles) and trichinellosis (Trichinella spiralis larvae encysting in skeletal muscle after undercooked pork or wild game, with myalgia, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia).

MS-13-H.t: Sequence fracture healing (hematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, remodeling) and predict delayed union from poor blood supply, infection, instability, smoking, diabetes, and malnutrition.
MS-13-H.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: fractures

MS-13-H.t: Predict complications of specific fractures: scaphoid and femoral neck (avascular necrosis from retrograde or retinacular blood supply), supracondylar humerus (brachial artery and median nerve), and long bone fractures (fat embolism with hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae).
MS-13-H.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: fractures

MS-13-H.t: Distinguish sprain (ligament), strain (muscle or tendon), contusion (soft tissue hemorrhage), and dislocation (loss of joint congruity), and explain why ligaments heal slowly.
MS-13-H.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: sprains, strains

MS-13-H.t: Explain compartment syndrome (rising pressure in a closed fascial compartment after fracture or crush, causing ischemia) and identify pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, preserved pulses early, and Volkmann ischemic contracture as a late result.
MS-13-H.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: compartment syndrome

MS-13-H.t: Explain rhabdomyolysis from crush injury, extreme exertion, or statins, and predict very high CK, myoglobinuria (dipstick positive for blood without red cells), hyperkalemia, and acute kidney injury.
MS-13-H.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: muscles, ligaments, fascia: rhabdomyolysis

MS-13-H.t: Describe myositis ossificans as heterotopic bone in muscle after trauma, and distinguish its zonal pattern (mature bone at the periphery) from osteosarcoma.
MS-13-H.usmle: Musculoskeletal: Degenerative and metabolic disorders: muscles, ligaments, fascia: muscle calcification and ossification
